title: BRICS Just Condemned the Pahalgam Attack — but the Real Fault Lines Were Everywhere Else
excerpt: India used its chairmanship to extract a unanimous terror condemnation from the bloc. The harder fights — over Gaza, tariffs, and China's conspicuous absence — exposed what BRICS still cannot agree on.
body:
When External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar convened BRICS foreign ministers in New Delhi on May 14 and 15, he had one non-negotiable outcome in mind: a collective condemnation of the April 2025 Pahalgam terrorist attack that killed 26 people, including several foreign tourists, in Indian-administered Kashmir.

He got it. The chair's statement — drafted by India and adopted without dissent — affirmed "zero tolerance for terrorism in all its forms and manifestations" and singled out the Pahalgam attack by name. For New Delhi, this was a diplomatic win worth the price of hosting. Getting Russia, China (albeit through its deputy), Brazil, South Africa, and a roster of newer BRICS members to name a terror attack on Indian soil is no small feat.

What the Statement Did — and Didn't — Say

The condemnation was unequivocal on terrorism, but the rest of the chair's statement revealed the fractures that define BRICS in 2026. On the Middle East, India walked a tightrope: the statement called for an "unconditional ceasefire" in Gaza and rejected "double standards in counter-terrorism" — language that pleased Arab members but stopped short of naming Israel. On trade, the ministers warned against "trade-distorting tariff policies," a clear reference to Washington's escalating duties — but carefully calibrated to avoid provoking the Trump administration during a period of active US-India bilateral negotiations.

China's Conspicuous Absence

The most telling signal came not from what was said but from who was missing. Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi did not attend in person, sending his deputy instead. The official reason was scheduling, but diplomats in New Delhi read it as a message: Beijing is not fully invested in India's BRICS presidency, particularly amid the ongoing border standoff along the Line of Actual Control.

India responded with characteristic pragmatism. Rather than draw attention to the snub, Jaishankar focused on deliverables — new working groups on climate resilience and digital public infrastructure, and a framework for BRICS cooperation on counterterrorism intelligence-sharing.

The Diaspora Angle

For the Indian diaspora, the Pahalgam condemnation carries particular resonance. The 2025 attack — which targeted tourists on the popular Baisaran Valley trek — sent shockwaves through NRI communities with family ties to Kashmir. A BRICS-level condemnation provides diplomatic ammunition that India has previously struggled to secure at the United Nations, where China and Russia have historically blocked or diluted India-backed terror designation efforts.

The broader BRICS dynamic matters too. With the bloc's expansion to include Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Egypt, Ethiopia, and Iran (though Tehran's participation remains complicated by the ongoing conflict), India's ability to steer the grouping's agenda is being tested. The September leaders' summit in New Delhi will be the real litmus test — and whether Xi Jinping accepts Modi's invitation in person will say more about the state of the relationship than any communiqué.

What to watch: The BRICS counterterrorism intelligence-sharing framework, if operationalized, would be India's most significant institutional achievement as chair. Expect details at the September summit.
